turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a tick, this login's slower than a wet week. Right. Ray, what are we seeing you for?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the cut from the operation. It's been... I don't know, doctor. It's not right.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm June, I come in as his carer. The hernia wound's red and it's leaking. I took the dressing off this morning.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hernia. Which side? The screen's still spinning, say it again.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Right side. They did it ten days back, I think. An open one.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Open right groin repair with mesh, ten days ago. The discharge letter's in my bag if you want it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ta. When did the redness actually start?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe a week? Or—
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, can I jump in? It looked alright until two days ago. Pink that day, and yesterday it was angry and wet.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Only two days? I thought it'd been looking funny for a week. I really don't know.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two days and a week. I won't nail the start. You mentioned leaking?
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yellow, a bit green. The gauze was soaked this morning. The smell was a little off, nothing shocking.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, it marks my singlet. And it stings when I walk.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any temperature with that?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night I was—
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold that thought, an alert just ate the notes. Go again?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Burning up last night. Hot and cold. This morning I just feel off, and I don't know if I've still got a temp, doctor.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): About ten last night, under the tongue, it was 38.4. He was sweaty. Cooler when I got there at eight this morning.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): 38.4. Mine says 37.6 now. Pulse is 96. Blood pressure is 138 over 82.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? I don't know what the numbers mean, doctor.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's not a high fever while you're sitting here. Is the pain just in the wound, or deeper in the belly?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the wound, sore if you touch it. Belly's alright, I think. I don't know.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting? Pain when you pass urine?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. Wee's fine. I had a bit of—
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry. No vomits at home either. Appetite's been pretty ordinary, not much of it, since the op, but he kept breakfast down.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): What antibiotics did the hospital send you home with?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Those capsules. I took them five days... or was it seven? I don't know, doctor. I think I finished them. Or I stopped.

[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The ones after the repair, by mouth. The label says cephalexin 500 milligrams, four times a day, for seven days. He stopped two days ago, and the lunchtime doses got skipped a lot. I can't say he took it properly.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen jumped back to the inbox. 500, four times a day? Once more.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Cephalexin, 500 milligrams, four times a day, by mouth, labelled for seven days. He's not taking it now.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any other tablets? Blood pressure stuff, blood thinners?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. There's a white one in the morning.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Perindopril 4 milligrams, once a day, by mouth, for his blood pressure. He had it this morning. No blood thinners.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perindopril 4, ta. Any allergies to medicines? Actually no, don't answer that yet, I should see the wound while I've got you. The clinic nurse isn't in. June, is the dressing already off?
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Just a fresh pad, it's not stuck. I can peel it back.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Lower end of the groin wound is red, about two centimetres out from the stitches, and it's tender, with yellow discharge at the bottom end. No fluctuance under it. Upper half is dry and healing, no red tracking up the tummy.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Does it look crook? I can't see down there.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not pretty. I'm not calling it a deep collection, and it could be a superficial wound infection or a stitch abscess. I won't decide it's spreading cellulitis from this look alone. Swab first, let's see what the test says before I lock anything in.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So, different tablets then? I don't even know if the first ones did anything.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll switch you to flucloxacillin for the wound, 500 milligrams, four times a day, by mouth, for seven days, on an empty stomach. Start this afternoon.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Four times a day is where he comes unstuck. I'll set alarms on the phone.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do. I'll take a wound swab now and send it to the lab. If the growth doesn't like fluclox, we'll change the antibiotic again. No blood test today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know what a swab even is, doctor.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): A cotton tip in the discharge, it's quick. The script's printing, and this printer's got a mind of its own.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): While that thing thinks, did you catch the cricket? That catch at deep midwicket, I nearly dropped my tea.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Highlights only. I thought it was the skipper, then I realised it was the sub. Ridiculous grab.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): I had it on and nodded off. Don't know the score, doctor.
[SEG0048] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Australia were four for plenty at drinks, then the storm rolled in. Hot northerly all afternoon and it bucketed down at tea.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): That northerly was filthy. I was late in, the West Gate was a car park from Spotswood right through.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): We came the back streets. Still took an age. Thursdays are worse, June reckons.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): They are. My grandson had nippers on Sunday, he's six, wouldn't get out of the water. Came home pink under the zinc, but he's not your patient, I'm just rabbiting.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Printer's alive. Ray, come back in two days and I'll check the wound again.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. And if it gets worse tonight? I don't know what I'm meant to do, doctor.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads, or the fever comes back, or you start vomiting, go to the emergency department tonight. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll change the pad each day and keep it dry. Baths are out, yeah?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Showers are fine, pat it dry, no soaking in the bath, and leave a pad on. Panadol for the sting if he needs it, his usual dose.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know if there's even Panadol at home, doctor.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There's a box in the cupboard. I'll pick the fluclox up from the chemist on the way out.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I still don't know if those first capsules were five days or seven, doctor.
[SEG0060] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The label was seven days. Whether every dose actually went in is another story.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stew on it. Two days here, or emergency if he goes downhill tonight. I've got to run, the next one's waiting and this machine's still spinning.

Cephalexin was labelled for seven days but lunchtime doses were missed, and it was never settled whether he actually took five or seven days.
Medicine allergy history was not obtained because the doctor deferred the question and never returned to it before prescribing flucloxacillin.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
